properties.name: A gate is run against the state it will be judged in — for the design export, that means AFTER committing
properties.statement:
Run a check against the state that will actually be judged, not against a working tree that is about to change. For `reflow2_check` specifically: **run it AFTER committing or amending, never before.**

WHY, MEASURED 2026-08-14 (`fact:the-lineage-gate-verdict-depends-on-when-you-run-it`): the lineage check compares the new export against the export committed at HEAD. Run before an amend it answers about a commit that is about to stop existing. The same file, byte-identical, FAILED at step 3 and PASSED at step 5 of one sequence — only `HEAD` moved between them.

THE GENERAL SHAPE: this gate always reasons about a PAIR of commits, and both of its known failure modes come from that pair differing between local and CI. `fact:the-local-lineage-gate-cannot-see-a-stacked-export` is the mirror image — the gate PASSING locally on a commit CI rejects, because CI checks out the PR merge commit where `HEAD~1` is main. Neither is a bug in the gate; both are a bug in when it is trusted.

ENFORCEMENT: **advisory, on Anthony's word 2026-08-14.** He was asked whether somebody who ran the gate early, trusted it and pushed should have been stopped, and answered that it is advice. The reasoning that supports it: a wrong local verdict is self-correcting, because CI checks out the merge commit and gives the authoritative answer either way — so this rule saves confusion and wasted cycles rather than preventing a bad landing. It also could not honestly be enforced: the ordering happens on a developer's machine and leaves no trace in the repository, so no check could see the violation.

DELIBERATELY NOT BOUND to a node with `GOVERNED_BY`. It shapes an operator's sequence rather than any design element, and `describe_schema` reports no edge type that models a DesignRule to what it governs here — the skill's instruction is to leave the edge out rather than assert one that is wrong.
